# rustdoc_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/

## Expand description

Rustdoc’s JSON output interface

These types are the public API exposed through the `--output-format json` flag. The [ Crate](https://docs.rs/struct.Crate.html)
struct is the root of the JSON blob and all other items are contained within.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

[§](https://docs.rs#rustc-hash)`rustc-hash`

We expose a `rustc-hash` feature, disabled by default. This feature switches the
[ std::collections::HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html) for [

`rustc_hash::FxHashMap`] to improve the performance of said
`HashMap` in specific situations.`cargo-semver-checks` for example, saw a [-3% improvement](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/266220-t-rustdoc/topic/rustc-hash.20and.20performance.20of.20rustdoc-types/near/474855731) when benchmarking using the
`aws_sdk_ec2` JSON output (~500MB of JSON). As always, we recommend measuring the impact before
turning this feature on, as [ FxHashMap](https://crates.io/crates/rustc-hash) only concerns itself with hash speed, and may
increase the number of collisions.

[§](https://docs.rs#rkyv_0_8)`rkyv_0_8`

We expose a `rkyv_0_8` feature, disabled by default. When enabled, it derives `rkyv`’s
[ Archive](https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.15/rkyv/trait.Archive.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.15/rkyv/trait.Serialize.html)

`Serialize`[traits for all types in this crate. Furthermore, it exposes the corresponding](https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.15/rkyv/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize``Archived*` types (e.g. `ArchivedId` for [).](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)

`Id``rkyv` lets you works with JSON output without paying the deserialization cost *upfront*,
thanks to [zero-copy deserialization](https://rkyv.org/zero-copy-deserialization.html).
You can perform various types of analyses on the `Archived*` version of the relevant types,
incurring the full deserialization cost only for the subset of items you actually need.

# serde_core 1.0.228 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/serde_core/1.0.228

The `serde_core` crate contains Serde's trait definitions with **no support for
#[derive()]**.

In crates that derive an implementation of `Serialize` or `Deserialize`, you
must depend on the [ serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) crate, not

`serde_core`.In crates that handwrite implementations of Serde traits, or only use them as
trait bounds, depending on `serde_core` is permitted. But `serde` re-exports all
of these traits and can be used for this use case too. If in doubt, disregard
`serde_core` and always use `serde`.

Crates that depend on `serde_core` instead of `serde` are able to compile in
parallel with `serde_derive` even when `serde`'s "derive" feature is turned on,
as shown in the following build timings.

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde` |
|---|

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde_core` |
|---|

# Serialize in serde_core::ser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/serde_core/1.0.228/target-redirect/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html

```
pub trait Serialize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[serialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize)<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), S::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where S: [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html);
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/index.html). All of
these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

`Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
type in your program. See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the
manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the [ linked-hash-map](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map) crate provides a

[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>``Serialize` for it.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.

See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the manual for more
information about how to implement this method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
// This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
impl Serialize for Person {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
        s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
        s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
        s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
        s.end()
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

This trait is implemented for tuples up to 16 items long.

# serde_core::ser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/index.html

## Expand description

Generic data structure serialization framework.

The two most important traits in this module are [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)

`Serializer`- **A type that implements**that can be serialized to any data format supported by Serde, and conversely- `Serialize`is a data structure
- **A type that implements**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.- `Serializer`is a data format

[§](https://docs.rs#the-serialize-trait)The Serialize trait

Serde provides [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html) implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is below. All of these can be
serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

[implementations for structs and enums in your program. See the](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)

`Serialize`[derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html) manually for
some type in your program. See the

[Implementing](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html)section of the manual for more about this.

`Serialize`Third-party crates may provide [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html) implementations for types that
they expose. For example the

[crate provides a](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map)

`linked-hash-map`[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>`[for it.](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)

`Serialize`[§](https://docs.rs#the-serializer-trait)The Serializer trait

[ Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html) implementations are provided by third-party crates, for
example

[,](https://github.com/serde-rs/json)

`serde_json`[and](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml)

`serde_yaml`[.](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard)

`postcard`A partial list of well-maintained formats is given on the [Serde
website](https://serde.rs/#data-formats).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementations-of-serialize-provided-by-serde)Implementations of Serialize provided by Serde

- **Primitive types**:- bool
- i8, i16, i32, i64, i128, isize
- u8, u16, u32, u64, u128, usize
- f32, f64
- char
- str
- &T and &mut T

- **Compound types**:- [T]
- [T; 0] through [T; 32]
- tuples up to size 16

- **Common standard library types**:- String
- Option<T>
- Result<T, E>
- PhantomData<T>

- **Wrapper types**:- Box<T>
- Cow<’a, T>
- Cell<T>
- RefCell<T>
- Mutex<T>
- RwLock<T>
- Rc<T> *(if*features = [“rc”]*is enabled)*
- Arc<T> *(if*features = [“rc”]*is enabled)*

- **Collection types**:- BTreeMap<K, V>
- BTreeSet<T>
- BinaryHeap<T>
- HashMap<K, V, H>
- HashSet<T, H>
- LinkedList<T>
- VecDeque<T>
- Vec<T>

- **FFI types**:- CStr
- CString
- OsStr
- OsString

- **Miscellaneous standard library types**:- Duration
- SystemTime
- Path
- PathBuf
- Range<T>
- RangeInclusive<T>
- Bound<T>
- num::NonZero*
- `!`- *(unstable)*

- **Net types**:- IpAddr
- Ipv4Addr
- Ipv6Addr
- SocketAddr
- SocketAddrV4
- SocketAddrV6

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use std::error::`- [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/error/trait.Error.html)as StdError;- `std`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Impossible](https://docs.rs/struct.Impossible.html)
- Helper type for implementing a `Serializer`that does not support serializing one of the compound types.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Error.html)
- Trait used by `Serialize`implementations to generically construct errors belonging to the`Serializer`against which they are currently running.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.SerializeMap.html)- Map
- Returned from `Serializer::serialize_map`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.SerializeSeq.html)- Seq
- Returned from `Serializer::serialize_seq`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.SerializeStruct.html)- Struct
- Returned from `Serializer::serialize_struct`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.SerializeStructVariant.html)- Struct - Variant
- Returned from `Serializer::serialize_struct_variant`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.SerializeTuple.html)- Tuple
- Returned from `Serializer::serialize_tuple`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.SerializeTupleStruct.html)- Tuple - Struct
- Returned from `Serializer::serialize_tuple_struct`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.SerializeTupleVariant.html)- Tuple - Variant
- Returned from `Serializer::serialize_tuple_variant`.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# serde_core/ser/mod.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Generic data structure serialization framework.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! The two most important traits in this module are [`Serialize`] and
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [`Serializer`].
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!  - **A type that implements `Serialize` is a data structure** that can be
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!    serialized to any data format supported by Serde, and conversely
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!  - **A type that implements `Serializer` is a data format** that can
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!    serialize any data structure supported by Serde.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! # The Serialize trait
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! Serde provides [`Serialize`] implementations for many Rust primitive and
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! standard library types. The complete list is below. All of these can be
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! serialized using Serde out of the box.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [`serde_derive`] to
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! automatically generate [`Serialize`] implementations for structs and enums
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! in your program. See the [derive section of the manual] for how to use this.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! In rare cases it may be necessary to implement [`Serialize`] manually for
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! some type in your program. See the [Implementing `Serialize`] section of the
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! manual for more about this.
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! Third-party crates may provide [`Serialize`] implementations for types that
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! they expose. For example the [`linked-hash-map`] crate provides a
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! [`LinkedHashMap<K, V>`] type that is serializable by Serde because the crate
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! provides an implementation of [`Serialize`] for it.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! # The Serializer trait
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! [`Serializer`] implementations are provided by third-party crates, for
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! example [`serde_json`], [`serde_yaml`] and [`postcard`].
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! A partial list of well-maintained formats is given on the [Serde
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! website][data formats].
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! # Implementations of Serialize provided by Serde
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!  - **Primitive types**:

[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!    - tuples up to size 16

[149](https://docs.rs#149)            /// Used when a [`Serialize`] implementation encounters any error
[150](https://docs.rs#150)            /// while serializing a type.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)            ///
[152](https://docs.rs#152)            /// The message should not be capitalized and should not end with a
[153](https://docs.rs#153)            /// period.
[154](https://docs.rs#154)            ///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)            /// For example, a filesystem [`Path`] may refuse to serialize
[156](https://docs.rs#156)            /// itself if it contains invalid UTF-8 data.
[157](https://docs.rs#157)            ///
[158](https://docs.rs#158)            /// ```edition2021
[159](https://docs.rs#159)            /// # struct Path;
[160](https://docs.rs#160)            /// #
[161](https://docs.rs#161)            /// # impl Path {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)            /// #     fn to_str(&self) -> Option<&str> {
[163](https://docs.rs#163)            /// #         unimplemented!()
[164](https://docs.rs#164)            /// #     }
[165](https://docs.rs#165)            /// # }
[166](https://docs.rs#166)            /// #
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            /// use serde::ser::{self, Serialize, Serializer};
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            ///
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            /// impl Serialize for Path {
[170](https://docs.rs#170)            ///     fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
[171](https://docs.rs#171)            ///     where
[172](https://docs.rs#172)            ///         S: Serializer,
[173](https://docs.rs#173)            ///     {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)            ///         match self.to_str() {
[175](https://docs.rs#175)            ///             Some(s) => serializer.serialize_str(s),
[176](https://docs.rs#176)            ///             None => Err(ser::Error::custom("path contains invalid UTF-8 characters")),
[177](https://docs.rs#177)            ///         }
[178](https://docs.rs#178)            ///     }
[179](https://docs.rs#179)            /// }
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            /// ```
[181](https://docs.rs#181)            ///
[182](https://docs.rs#182)            /// [`Path`]: std::path::Path
[183](https://docs.rs#183)            /// [`Serialize`]: crate::Serialize
[184](https://docs.rs#184)            fn custom<T>(msg: T) -> Self
[185](https://docs.rs#185)            where
[186](https://docs.rs#186)                T: Display;
[187](https://docs.rs#187)        }
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    }

[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// by Serde.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)///
[202](https://docs.rs#202)/// Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
[203](https://docs.rs#203)/// standard library types. The complete list is [here][crate::ser]. All of
[204](https://docs.rs#204)/// these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)///
[206](https://docs.rs#206)/// Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [`serde_derive`] to
[207](https://docs.rs#207)/// automatically generate `Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
[208](https://docs.rs#208)/// your program. See the [derive section of the manual] for how to use this.
[209](https://docs.rs#209)///
[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// type in your program. See the [Implementing `Serialize`] section of the
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// manual for more about this.
[213](https://docs.rs#213)///
[214](https://docs.rs#214)/// Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// they expose. For example the [`linked-hash-map`] crate provides a
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// [`LinkedHashMap<K, V>`] type that is serializable by Serde because the crate
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// provides an implementation of `Serialize` for it.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// [Implementing `Serialize`]: https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// [`LinkedHashMap<K, V>`]: https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// [`linked-hash-map`]: https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// [`serde_derive`]: https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// [derive section of the manual]: https://serde.rs/derive.html
[224](https://docs.rs#224)#[cfg_attr(
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        // Prevents `serde_core::ser::Serialize` appearing in the error message
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        // in projects with no direct dependency on serde_core.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::Serialize` is not satisfied",
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        note = "for local types consider adding `#[derive(serde::Serialize)]` to your `{Self}` type",
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        note = "for types from other crates check whether the crate offers a `serde` feature flag",
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    )

[234](https://docs.rs#234)pub trait [Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/trait.Serialize.html) {
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    ///
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    /// See the [Implementing `Serialize`] section of the manual for more
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    /// information about how to implement this method.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    ///
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    /// ```edition2021
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    ///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// struct Person {
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    ///     name: String,
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    ///     age: u8,
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    ///     phones: Vec<String>,
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// }
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    ///
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    /// // This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    /// impl Serialize for Person {
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    ///     fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    ///     where
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    ///         S: Serializer,
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    ///     {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    ///         let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    ///         s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    ///         s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///         s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    ///         s.end()
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    ///     }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// }
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// ```
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    ///
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    /// [Implementing `Serialize`]: https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::Ok, S::Error>
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    where
[267](https://docs.rs#267)        S: [Serializer](https://docs.rs#355-1462);
[268](https://docs.rs#268)}

[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)/// A **data format** that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)///
[274](https://docs.rs#274)/// The role of this trait is to define the serialization half of the [Serde
[275](https://docs.rs#275)/// data model], which is a way to categorize every Rust data structure into one
[276](https://docs.rs#276)/// of 29 possible types. Each method of the `Serializer` trait corresponds to
[277](https://docs.rs#277)/// one of the types of the data model.
[278](https://docs.rs#278)///
[279](https://docs.rs#279)/// Implementations of `Serialize` map themselves into this data model by
[280](https://docs.rs#280)/// invoking exactly one of the `Serializer` methods.
[281](https://docs.rs#281)///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)/// The types that make up the Serde data model are:
[283](https://docs.rs#283)///
[284](https://docs.rs#284)///  - **14 primitive types**
[285](https://docs.rs#285)///    - bool
[286](https://docs.rs#286)///    - i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
[287](https://docs.rs#287)///    - u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
[288](https://docs.rs#288)///    - f32, f64
[289](https://docs.rs#289)///    - char
[290](https://docs.rs#290)///  - **string**
[291](https://docs.rs#291)///    - UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
[292](https://docs.rs#292)///    - When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing,
[293](https://docs.rs#293)///      there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.
[294](https://docs.rs#294)///  - **byte array** - \[u8\]
[295](https://docs.rs#295)///    - Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be
[296](https://docs.rs#296)///      transient, owned, or borrowed.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)///  - **option**
[298](https://docs.rs#298)///    - Either none or some value.
[299](https://docs.rs#299)///  - **unit**
[300](https://docs.rs#300)///    - The type of `()` in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing
[301](https://docs.rs#301)///      no data.
[302](https://docs.rs#302)///  - **unit_struct**
[303](https://docs.rs#303)///    - For example `struct Unit` or `PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named
[304](https://docs.rs#304)///      value containing no data.
[305](https://docs.rs#305)///  - **unit_variant**
[306](https://docs.rs#306)///    - For example the `E::A` and `E::B` in `enum E { A, B }`.
[307](https://docs.rs#307)///  - **newtype_struct**
[308](https://docs.rs#308)///    - For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.
[309](https://docs.rs#309)///  - **newtype_variant**
[310](https://docs.rs#310)///    - For example the `E::N` in `enum E { N(u8) }`.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)///  - **seq**
[312](https://docs.rs#312)///    - A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
[313](https://docs.rs#313)///      `Vec<T>` or `HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not
[314](https://docs.rs#314)///      be known before iterating through all the data. When deserializing,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)///      the length is determined by looking at the serialized data.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)///  - **tuple**
[317](https://docs.rs#317)///    - A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
[318](https://docs.rs#318)///      length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
[319](https://docs.rs#319)///      serialized data, for example `(u8,)` or `(String, u64, Vec<T>)` or
[320](https://docs.rs#320)///      `[u64; 10]`.
[321](https://docs.rs#321)///  - **tuple_struct**
[322](https://docs.rs#322)///    - A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.
[323](https://docs.rs#323)///  - **tuple_variant**
[324](https://docs.rs#324)///    - For example the `E::T` in `enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.
[325](https://docs.rs#325)///  - **map**
[326](https://docs.rs#326)///    - A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)///  - **struct**
[328](https://docs.rs#328)///    - A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
[329](https://docs.rs#329)///      will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
[330](https://docs.rs#330)///      serialized data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.
[331](https://docs.rs#331)///  - **struct_variant**
[332](https://docs.rs#332)///    - For example the `E::S` in `enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.
[333](https://docs.rs#333)///
[334](https://docs.rs#334)/// Many Serde serializers produce text or binary data as output, for example
[335](https://docs.rs#335)/// JSON or Postcard. This is not a requirement of the `Serializer` trait, and
[336](https://docs.rs#336)/// there are serializers that do not produce text or binary output. One example
[337](https://docs.rs#337)/// is the `serde_json::value::Serializer` (distinct from the main `serde_json`
[338](https://docs.rs#338)/// serializer) that produces a `serde_json::Value` data structure in memory as
[339](https://docs.rs#339)/// output.
[340](https://docs.rs#340)///
[341](https://docs.rs#341)/// [Serde data model]: https://serde.rs/data-model.html
[342](https://docs.rs#342)///
[343](https://docs.rs#343)/// # Example implementation
[344](https://docs.rs#344)///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// The [example data format] presented on the website contains example code for
[346](https://docs.rs#346)/// a basic JSON `Serializer`.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)///
[348](https://docs.rs#348)/// [example data format]: https://serde.rs/data-format.html
[349](https://docs.rs#349)#[cfg_attr(
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[352](https://docs.rs#352)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::Serializer` is not satisfied",
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    )
[354](https://docs.rs#354))]

[356](https://docs.rs#356)    /// The output type produced by this `Serializer` during successful
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    /// serialization. Most serializers that produce text or binary output
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    /// should set `Ok = ()` and serialize into an [`io::Write`] or buffer
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    /// contained within the `Serializer` instance. Serializers that build
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// in-memory data structures may be simplified by using `Ok` to propagate
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// the data structure around.
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    ///
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// [`io::Write`]: std::io::Write
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    type Ok;

[722](https://docs.rs#722)    /// Serialize a chunk of raw byte data.
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    ///
[724](https://docs.rs#724)    /// Enables serializers to serialize byte slices more compactly or more
[725](https://docs.rs#725)    /// efficiently than other types of slices. If no efficient implementation
[726](https://docs.rs#726)    /// is available, a reasonable implementation would be to forward to
[727](https://docs.rs#727)    /// `serialize_seq`. If forwarded, the implementation looks usually just
[728](https://docs.rs#728)    /// like this:
[729](https://docs.rs#729)    ///
[730](https://docs.rs#730)    /// ```edition2021
[731](https://docs.rs#731)    /// # use serde::ser::{Serializer, SerializeSeq};
[732](https://docs.rs#732)    /// # use serde_core::__private::doc::Error;
[733](https://docs.rs#733)    /// #
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    /// # struct MySerializer;
[735](https://docs.rs#735)    /// #
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    /// # impl Serializer for MySerializer {
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    /// #     type Ok = ();
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    /// #     type Error = Error;
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    /// #
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    /// fn serialize_bytes(self, v: &[u8]) -> Result<Self::Ok, Self::Error> {
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    ///     let mut seq = self.serialize_seq(Some(v.len()))?;
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    ///     for b in v {
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    ///         seq.serialize_element(b)?;
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    ///     }
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    ///     seq.end()
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    /// }
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    /// #
[748](https://docs.rs#748)    /// #     serde_core::__serialize_unimplemented! {
[749](https://docs.rs#749)    /// #         bool i8 i16 i32 i64 u8 u16 u32 u64 f32 f64 char str none some
[750](https://docs.rs#750)    /// #         unit unit_struct unit_variant newtype_struct newtype_variant
[751](https://docs.rs#751)    /// #         seq tuple tuple_struct tuple_variant map struct struct_variant
[752](https://docs.rs#752)    /// #     }
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    /// # }
[754](https://docs.rs#754)    /// ```
[755](https://docs.rs#755)    fn serialize_bytes(self, v: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::Ok, Self::Error>;

[924](https://docs.rs#924)    /// Serialize a newtype variant like `E::N` in `enum E { N(u8) }`.

[937](https://docs.rs#937)    ///

[959](https://docs.rs#959)
[960](https://docs.rs#960)    /// Begin to serialize a variably sized sequence. This call must be
[961](https://docs.rs#961)    /// followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`, then a call to
[962](https://docs.rs#962)    /// `end`.
[963](https://docs.rs#963)    ///
[964](https://docs.rs#964)    /// The argument is the number of elements in the sequence, which may or may
[965](https://docs.rs#965)    /// not be computable before the sequence is iterated. Some serializers only
[966](https://docs.rs#966)    /// support sequences whose length is known up front.
[967](https://docs.rs#967)    ///
[968](https://docs.rs#968)    /// ```edition2021
[969](https://docs.rs#969)    /// # use std::marker::PhantomData;
[970](https://docs.rs#970)    /// #
[971](https://docs.rs#971)    /// # struct Vec<T>(PhantomData<T>);
[972](https://docs.rs#972)    /// #
[973](https://docs.rs#973)    /// # impl<T> Vec<T> {
[974](https://docs.rs#974)    /// #     fn len(&self) -> usize {
[975](https://docs.rs#975)    /// #         unimplemented!()
[976](https://docs.rs#976)    /// #     }
[977](https://docs.rs#977)    /// # }
[978](https://docs.rs#978)    /// #
[979](https://docs.rs#979)    /// # impl<'a, T> IntoIterator for &'a Vec<T> {
[980](https://docs.rs#980)    /// #     type Item = &'a T;
[981](https://docs.rs#981)    /// #     type IntoIter = Box<dyn Iterator<Item = &'a T>>;
[982](https://docs.rs#982)    /// #
[983](https://docs.rs#983)    /// #     fn into_iter(self) -> Self::IntoIter {
[984](https://docs.rs#984)    /// #         unimplemented!()
[985](https://docs.rs#985)    /// #     }
[986](https://docs.rs#986)    /// # }
[987](https://docs.rs#987)    /// #
[988](https://docs.rs#988)    /// use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeSeq, Serializer};
[989](https://docs.rs#989)    ///
[990](https://docs.rs#990)    /// impl<T> Serialize for Vec<T>
[991](https://docs.rs#991)    /// where
[992](https://docs.rs#992)    ///     T: Serialize,
[993](https://docs.rs#993)    /// {
[994](https://docs.rs#994)    ///     fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
[995](https://docs.rs#995)    ///     where
[996](https://docs.rs#996)    ///         S: Serializer,
[997](https://docs.rs#997)    ///     {
[998](https://docs.rs#998)    ///         let mut seq = serializer.serialize_seq(Some(self.len()))?;
[999](https://docs.rs#999)    ///         for element in self {
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)    ///             seq.serialize_element(element)?;
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)    ///         }
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)    ///         seq.end()
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)    ///     }
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)    /// }
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)    /// ```
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)    fn serialize_seq(self, len: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)>) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::SerializeSeq, Self::Error>;

[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)    /// Begin to serialize a statically sized sequence whose length will be

[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)    ///

[1033](https://docs.rs#1033)    ///     {
[1034](https://docs.rs#1034)    ///         let mut tup = serializer.serialize_tuple(3)?;
[1035](https://docs.rs#1035)    ///         tup.serialize_element(&self.0)?;
[1036](https://docs.rs#1036)    ///         tup.serialize_element(&self.1)?;
[1037](https://docs.rs#1037)    ///         tup.serialize_element(&self.2)?;

[1042](https://docs.rs#1042)    ///
[1043](https://docs.rs#1043)    /// ```edition2021

[1245](https://docs.rs#1245)    ///     where
[1246](https://docs.rs#1246)    ///         S: Serializer,
[1247](https://docs.rs#1247)    ///     {
[1248](https://docs.rs#1248)    ///         match *self {
[1249](https://docs.rs#1249)    ///             E::S {
[1250](https://docs.rs#1250)    ///                 ref r,
[1251](https://docs.rs#1251)    ///                 ref g,
[1252](https://docs.rs#1252)    ///                 ref b,
[1253](https://docs.rs#1253)    ///             } => {
[1254](https://docs.rs#1254)    ///                 let mut sv = serializer.serialize_struct_variant("E", 0, "S", 3)?;
[1255](https://docs.rs#1255)    ///                 sv.serialize_field("r", r)?;
[1256](https://docs.rs#1256)    ///                 sv.serialize_field("g", g)?;
[1257](https://docs.rs#1257)    ///                 sv.serialize_field("b", b)?;
[1258](https://docs.rs#1258)    ///                 sv.end()
[1259](https://docs.rs#1259)    ///             }
[1260](https://docs.rs#1260)    ///         }
[1261](https://docs.rs#1261)    ///     }
[1262](https://docs.rs#1262)    /// }
[1263](https://docs.rs#1263)    /// ```
[1264](https://docs.rs#1264)    fn serialize_struct_variant(
[1265](https://docs.rs#1265)        self,
[1266](https://docs.rs#1266)        name: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
[1267](https://docs.rs#1267)        variant_index: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u32.html),
[1268](https://docs.rs#1268)        variant: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
[1269](https://docs.rs#1269)        len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
[1270](https://docs.rs#1270)    ) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::SerializeStructVariant, Self::Error>;

[1410](https://docs.rs#1410)    /// Determine whether `Serialize` implementations should serialize in
[1411](https://docs.rs#1411)    /// human-readable form.
[1412](https://docs.rs#1412)    ///
[1413](https://docs.rs#1413)    /// Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to
[1414](https://docs.rs#1414)    /// construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient.
[1415](https://docs.rs#1415)    /// Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the
[1416](https://docs.rs#1416)    /// human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the
[1417](https://docs.rs#1417)    /// compact one.
[1418](https://docs.rs#1418)    ///
[1419](https://docs.rs#1419)    /// ```edition2021
[1420](https://docs.rs#1420)    /// # use std::fmt::{self, Display};
[1421](https://docs.rs#1421)    /// #
[1422](https://docs.rs#1422)    /// # struct Timestamp;
[1423](https://docs.rs#1423)    /// #
[1424](https://docs.rs#1424)    /// # impl Timestamp {
[1425](https://docs.rs#1425)    /// #     fn seconds_since_epoch(&self) -> u64 { unimplemented!() }
[1426](https://docs.rs#1426)    /// # }
[1427](https://docs.rs#1427)    /// #
[1428](https://docs.rs#1428)    /// # impl Display for Timestamp {
[1429](https://docs.rs#1429)    /// #     fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[1430](https://docs.rs#1430)    /// #         unimplemented!()
[1431](https://docs.rs#1431)    /// #     }
[1432](https://docs.rs#1432)    /// # }
[1433](https://docs.rs#1433)    /// #
[1434](https://docs.rs#1434)    /// use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
[1435](https://docs.rs#1435)    ///
[1436](https://docs.rs#1436)    /// impl Serialize for Timestamp {
[1437](https://docs.rs#1437)    ///     fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
[1438](https://docs.rs#1438)    ///     where
[1439](https://docs.rs#1439)    ///         S: Serializer,
[1440](https://docs.rs#1440)    ///     {
[1441](https://docs.rs#1441)    ///         if serializer.is_human_readable() {
[1442](https://docs.rs#1442)    ///             // Serialize to a human-readable string "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
[1443](https://docs.rs#1443)    ///             self.to_string().serialize(serializer)
[1444](https://docs.rs#1444)    ///         } else {
[1445](https://docs.rs#1445)    ///             // Serialize to a compact binary representation.
[1446](https://docs.rs#1446)    ///             self.seconds_since_epoch().serialize(serializer)
[1447](https://docs.rs#1447)    ///         }
[1448](https://docs.rs#1448)    ///     }
[1449](https://docs.rs#1449)    /// }
[1450](https://docs.rs#1450)    /// ```
[1451](https://docs.rs#1451)    ///
[1452](https://docs.rs#1452)    /// The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
[1453](https://docs.rs#1453)    /// may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
[1454](https://docs.rs#1454)    /// support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
[1455](https://docs.rs#1455)    /// human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
[1456](https://docs.rs#1456)    /// change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
[1457](https://docs.rs#1457)    /// deserialize from the same data in compact mode.
[1458](https://docs.rs#1458)    #[inline]
[1459](https://docs.rs#1459)    fn is_human_readable(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html) {
[1460](https://docs.rs#1460)        true
[1461](https://docs.rs#1461)    }
[1462](https://docs.rs#1462)}
[1463](https://docs.rs#1463)
[1464](https://docs.rs#1464)/// Returned from `Serializer::serialize_seq`.

[1811](https://docs.rs#1811)pub trait [SerializeMap](https://docs.rs/serde_core/ser/trait.SerializeMap.html) {
[1812](https://docs.rs#1812)    /// Must match the `Ok` type of our `Serializer`.
[1813](https://docs.rs#1813)    type Ok;
[1814](https://docs.rs#1814)
[1815](https://docs.rs#1815)    /// Must match the `Error` type of our `Serializer`.
[1816](https://docs.rs#1816)    type Error: [Error](https://docs.rs#192);
[1817](https://docs.rs#1817)
[1818](https://docs.rs#1818)    /// Serialize a map key.
[1819](https://docs.rs#1819)    ///
[1820](https://docs.rs#1820)    /// If possible, `Serialize` implementations are encouraged to use
[1821](https://docs.rs#1821)    /// `serialize_entry` instead as it may be implemented more efficiently in
[1822](https://docs.rs#1822)    /// some formats compared to a pair of calls to `serialize_key` and
[1823](https://docs.rs#1823)    /// `serialize_value`.
[1824](https://docs.rs#1824)    fn serialize_key<T>(&mut self, key: &T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<(), Self::Error>
[1825](https://docs.rs#1825)    where
[1826](https://docs.rs#1826)        T: ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) + [Serialize](https://docs.rs#234-268);
[1827](https://docs.rs#1827)
[1828](https://docs.rs#1828)    /// Serialize a map value.
[1829](https://docs.rs#1829)    ///
[1830](https://docs.rs#1830)    /// # Panics
[1831](https://docs.rs#1831)    ///
[1832](https://docs.rs#1832)    /// Calling `serialize_value` before `serialize_key` is incorrect and is
[1833](https://docs.rs#1833)    /// allowed to panic or produce bogus results.
[1834](https://docs.rs#1834)    fn serialize_value<T>(&mut self, value: &T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<(), Self::Error>
[1835](https://docs.rs#1835)    where
[1836](https://docs.rs#1836)        T: ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) + [Serialize](https://docs.rs#234-268);
[1837](https://docs.rs#1837)
[1838](https://docs.rs#1838)    /// Serialize a map entry consisting of a key and a value.
[1839](https://docs.rs#1839)    ///
[1840](https://docs.rs#1840)    /// Some [`Serialize`] types are not able to hold a key and value in memory
[1841](https://docs.rs#1841)    /// at the same time so `SerializeMap` implementations are required to
[1842](https://docs.rs#1842)    /// support [`serialize_key`] and [`serialize_value`] individually. The
[1843](https://docs.rs#1843)    /// `serialize_entry` method allows serializers to optimize for the case
[1844](https://docs.rs#1844)    /// where key and value are both available. [`Serialize`] implementations
[1845](https://docs.rs#1845)    /// are encouraged to use `serialize_entry` if possible.
[1846](https://docs.rs#1846)    ///
[1847](https://docs.rs#1847)    /// The default implementation delegates to [`serialize_key`] and
[1848](https://docs.rs#1848)    /// [`serialize_value`]. This is appropriate for serializers that do not
[1849](https://docs.rs#1849)    /// care about performance or are not able to optimize `serialize_entry` any
[1850](https://docs.rs#1850)    /// better than this.
[1851](https://docs.rs#1851)    ///
[1852](https://docs.rs#1852)    /// [`Serialize`]: crate::Serialize
[1853](https://docs.rs#1853)    /// [`serialize_key`]: Self::serialize_key
[1854](https://docs.rs#1854)    /// [`serialize_value`]: Self::serialize_value
[1855](https://docs.rs#1855)    fn serialize_entry<K, V>(&mut self, key: &K, value: &V) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<(), Self::Error>
[1856](https://docs.rs#1856)    where
[1857](https://docs.rs#1857)        K: ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) + [Serialize](https://docs.rs#234-268),
[1858](https://docs.rs#1858)        V: ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) + [Serialize](https://docs.rs#234-268),
[1859](https://docs.rs#1859)    {
[1860](https://docs.rs#1860)        [tri!](https://docs.rs/lib.rs.html#111)(self.serialize_key(key));
[1861](https://docs.rs#1861)        [self](https://docs.rs#1855).[serialize_value](https://docs.rs#1834-1836)([value](https://docs.rs#1855))
[1862](https://docs.rs#1862)    }
[1863](https://docs.rs#1863)
[1864](https://docs.rs#1864)    /// Finish serializing a map.
[1865](https://docs.rs#1865)    fn end(self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::Ok, Self::Error>;
[1866](https://docs.rs#1866)}
[1867](https://docs.rs#1867)
[1868](https://docs.rs#1868)/// Returned from `Serializer::serialize_struct`.
[1869](https://docs.rs#1869)///
[1870](https://docs.rs#1870)/// # Example use
[1871](https://docs.rs#1871)///
[1872](https://docs.rs#1872)/// ```edition2021
[1873](https://docs.rs#1873)/// use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
[1874](https://docs.rs#1874)///

[1876](https://docs.rs#1876)///     r: u8,

[1879](https://docs.rs#1879)/// }

}## Expand description

A **data format** that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

The role of this trait is to define the serialization half of the [Serde
data model](https://serde.rs/data-model.html), which is a way to categorize every Rust data structure into one
of 29 possible types. Each method of the `Serializer` trait corresponds to
one of the types of the data model.

Implementations of `Serialize` map themselves into this data model by
invoking exactly one of the `Serializer` methods.

The types that make up the Serde data model are:

- **14 primitive types**- bool
- i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
- u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
- f32, f64
- char

- **string**- UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
- When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing, there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.

- **byte array**- [u8]- Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be transient, owned, or borrowed.

- **option**- Either none or some value.

- **unit**- The type of `()`in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing no data.

- The type of
- **unit_struct**- For example `struct Unit`or`PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named value containing no data.

- For example
- **unit_variant**- For example the `E::A`and`E::B`in`enum E { A, B }`.

- For example the
- **newtype_struct**- For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

- For example
- **newtype_variant**- For example the `E::N`in`enum E { N(u8) }`.

- For example the
- **seq**- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
`Vec<T>`or`HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not be known before iterating through all the data. When deserializing, the length is determined by looking at the serialized data.

- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
- **tuple**- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `(u8,)`or`(String, u64, Vec<T>)`or`[u64; 10]`.

- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **tuple_struct**- A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.

- A named tuple, for example
- **tuple_variant**- For example the `E::T`in`enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.

- For example the
- **map**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example
- **struct**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **struct_variant**- For example the `E::S`in`enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.

- For example the

Many Serde serializers produce text or binary data as output, for example
JSON or Postcard. This is not a requirement of the `Serializer` trait, and
there are serializers that do not produce text or binary output. One example
is the `serde_json::value::Serializer` (distinct from the main `serde_json`
serializer) that produces a `serde_json::Value` data structure in memory as
output.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-implementation)Example implementation

The [example data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html) presented on the website contains example code for
a basic JSON `Serializer`.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

The output type produced by this `Serializer` during successful
serialization. Most serializers that produce text or binary output
should set `Ok = ()` and serialize into an [ io::Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html) or buffer
contained within the

`Serializer` instance. Serializers that build
in-memory data structures may be simplified by using `Ok` to propagate
the data structure around.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize an `i8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i8` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i16` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i32` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize a `u8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u8` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u16` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u32` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize an `f32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `f32` and `f64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `f64` and
forward to `serialize_f64`.

Serialize a character.

If the format does not support characters, it is reasonable to serialize
it as a single element `str` or a `u32`.

Serialize a chunk of raw byte data.

Enables serializers to serialize byte slices more compactly or more
efficiently than other types of slices. If no efficient implementation
is available, a reasonable implementation would be to forward to
`serialize_seq`. If forwarded, the implementation looks usually just
like this:

Serialize a unit struct like `struct Unit` or `PhantomData<T>`.

A reasonable implementation would be to forward to `serialize_unit`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Nothing;
impl Serialize for Nothing {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_unit_struct("Nothing")
    }
}
```

Serialize a unit variant like `E::A` in `enum E { A, B }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, and the `variant` is the name of the
variant.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
enum E {
    A,
    B,
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::A => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 0, "A"),
            E::B => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 1, "B"),
        }
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#916-922)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#916-922)

Serialize a newtype struct like `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

Serializers are encouraged to treat newtype structs as insignificant
wrappers around the data they contain. A reasonable implementation would
be to forward to `value.serialize(self)`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Millimeters(u8);
impl Serialize for Millimeters {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_newtype_struct("Millimeters", &self.0)
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#950-958)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#950-958)

Serialize a newtype variant like `E::N` in `enum E { N(u8) }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, and the `variant` is the name of the
variant. The `value` is the data contained within this newtype variant.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
enum E {
    M(String),
    N(u8),
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::M(ref s) => serializer.serialize_newtype_variant("E", 0, "M", s),
            E::N(n) => serializer.serialize_newtype_variant("E", 1, "N", &n),
        }
    }
}

#### fn [serialize_seq](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_seq)(
    self,
    len: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)>,

Begin to serialize a variably sized sequence. This call must be
followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`, then a call to
`end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the sequence, which may or may not be computable before the sequence is iterated. Some serializers only support sequences whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeSeq, Serializer};
impl<T> Serialize for Vec<T>
where
    T: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_seq(Some(self.len()))?;
        for element in self {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}
```

Begin to serialize a statically sized sequence whose length will be
known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized data.
This call must be followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`,
then a call to `end`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTuple, Serializer};
impl<A, B, C> Serialize for (A, B, C)
where
    A: Serialize,
    B: Serialize,
    C: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut tup = serializer.serialize_tuple(3)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.0)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.1)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.2)?;
        tup.end()
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTuple, Serializer};
const VRAM_SIZE: usize = 386;
struct Vram([u16; VRAM_SIZE]);
impl Serialize for Vram {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_tuple(VRAM_SIZE)?;
        for element in &self.0[..] {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}

    where
        S: Serializer,

                tv.serialize_field(a)?;
                tv.serialize_field(b)?;
                tv.end()

            E::U(ref a, ref b, ref c) => {
                let mut tv = serializer.serialize_tuple_variant("E", 1, "U", 3)?;
                tv.serialize_field(a)?;
                tv.serialize_field(b)?;
                tv.serialize_field(c)?;
                tv.end()

Begin to serialize a map. This call must be followed by zero or more
calls to `serialize_key` and `serialize_value`, then a call to `end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the map, which may or may not be computable before the map is iterated. Some serializers only support maps whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeMap, Serializer};
impl<K, V> Serialize for HashMap<K, V>
where
    K: Serialize,
    V: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut map = serializer.serialize_map(Some(self.len()))?;
        for (k, v) in self {
            map.serialize_entry(k, v)?;
        }
        map.end()
    }
}
```

This call must be followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_field`,

```

struct Rgb {
    r: u8,
    g: u8,
    b: u8,
}
impl Serialize for Rgb {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut rgb = serializer.serialize_struct("Rgb", 3)?;
        rgb.serialize_field("r", &self.r)?;
        rgb.serialize_field("g", &self.g)?;
        rgb.serialize_field("b", &self.b)?;
        rgb.end()
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#1264-1270)#### fn [serialize_struct_variant](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_struct_variant)(
    self,
    name: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    variant_index: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u32.html),
    variant: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeStructVariant](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeStructVariant), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#1264-1270)

#### fn [serialize_struct_variant](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_struct_variant)(
    self,
    name: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    variant_index: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u32.html),
    variant: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeStructVariant](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeStructVariant), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Begin to serialize a struct variant like `E::S` in `enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`. This call must be followed by zero or more calls to
`serialize_field`, then a call to `end`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, the `variant` is the name of the variant,
and the `len` is the number of data fields that will be serialized.
`len` does not include fields which are skipped with
[ SerializeStructVariant::skip_field](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.SerializeStructVariant.html#method.skip_field).

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStructVariant, Serializer};
enum E {
    S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 },
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::S {
                ref r,
                ref g,
                ref b,
            } => {
                let mut sv = serializer.serialize_struct_variant("E", 0, "S", 3)?;
                sv.serialize_field("r", r)?;
                sv.serialize_field("g", g)?;
                sv.serialize_field("b", b)?;
                sv.end()
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Collect an iterator as a sequence.

The default implementation serializes each item yielded by the iterator
using [ serialize_seq](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_seq). Implementors should not need to override this
method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct SecretlyOneHigher {
    data: Vec<i32>,
}
impl Serialize for SecretlyOneHigher {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_seq(self.data.iter().map(|x| x + 1))
    }
}

use std::collections::BTreeSet;
struct MapToUnit {
    keys: BTreeSet<i32>,
}
// Serializes as a map in which the values are all unit.
impl Serialize for MapToUnit {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_map(self.keys.iter().map(|k| (k, ())))
    }
}

use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
impl Serialize for DateTime {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_str(&format_args!("{:?}{:?}", self.naive_local(), self.offset()))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)

#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

Determine whether `Serialize` implementations should serialize in
human-readable form.

Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient. Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the compact one.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
impl Serialize for Timestamp {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        if serializer.is_human_readable() {
            // Serialize to a human-readable string "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
            self.to_string().serialize(serializer)
        } else {
            // Serialize to a compact binary representation.
            self.seconds_since_epoch().serialize(serializer)
        }
    }
}
```
The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
deserialize from the same data in compact mode.

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

Creates an empty linked hash map with the given initial capacity and hash builder.

Reserves capacity for at least `additional` more elements to be inserted into the map. The
map may reserve more space to avoid frequent allocations.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the new allocation size overflows `usize.`

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/linked_hash_map/lib.rs.html#227-230)#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/linked_hash_map/lib.rs.html#227-230)

#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

Shrinks the capacity of the map as much as possible. It will drop down as much as possible while maintaining the internal rules and possibly leaving some space in accordance with the resize policy.

Gets the given key’s corresponding entry in the map for in-place manipulation.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut letters = LinkedHashMap::new();
for ch in "a short treatise on fungi".chars() {
    let counter = letters.entry(ch).or_insert(0);
    *counter += 1;
}
assert_eq!(letters[&'s'], 2);
assert_eq!(letters[&'t'], 3);
assert_eq!(letters[&'u'], 1);
assert_eq!(letters.get(&'y'), None);
```
Returns an iterator visiting all entries in insertion order.
Iterator element type is `OccupiedEntry<K, V, S>`. Allows for removal
as well as replacing the entry.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert("a", 10);
map.insert("c", 30);
map.insert("b", 20);
{
    let mut iter = map.entries();
    let mut entry = iter.next().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(&"a", entry.key());
    *entry.get_mut() = 17;
}
assert_eq!(&17, map.get(&"a").unwrap());
```
Inserts a key-value pair into the map. If the key already existed, the old value is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert(1, "a");
map.insert(2, "b");
assert_eq!(map[&1], "a");
assert_eq!(map[&2], "b");
```
Returns the value corresponding to the key in the map.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert(1, "a");
map.insert(2, "b");
map.insert(2, "c");
map.insert(3, "d");
assert_eq!(map.get(&1), Some(&"a"));
assert_eq!(map.get(&2), Some(&"c"));
```
Returns the mutable reference corresponding to the key in the map.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert(1, "a");
map.insert(2, "b");
*map.get_mut(&1).unwrap() = "c";
assert_eq!(map.get(&1), Some(&"c"));
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/linked_hash_map/lib.rs.html#431-445)#### pub fn [get_refresh](https://docs.rs#method.get_refresh)<Q>(&mut self, k: [&Q](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[&mut V](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/linked_hash_map/lib.rs.html#431-445)

#### pub fn [get_refresh](https://docs.rs#method.get_refresh)<Q>(&mut self, k: [&Q](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[&mut V](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)>

Returns the value corresponding to the key in the map.

If value is found, it is moved to the end of the list. This operation can be used in implemenation of LRU cache.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert(1, "a");
map.insert(2, "b");
map.insert(3, "d");
assert_eq!(map.get_refresh(&2), Some(&mut "b"));
assert_eq!((&2, &"b"), map.iter().rev().next().unwrap());
```
Removes and returns the value corresponding to the key from the map.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert(2, "a");
assert_eq!(map.remove(&1), None);
assert_eq!(map.remove(&2), Some("a"));
assert_eq!(map.remove(&2), None);
assert_eq!(map.len(), 0);
```
Returns the maximum number of key-value pairs the map can hold without reallocating.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map: LinkedHashMap<i32, &str> = LinkedHashMap::new();
let capacity = map.capacity();
```
Removes the first entry.

Can be used in implementation of LRU cache.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert(1, 10);
map.insert(2, 20);
map.pop_front();
assert_eq!(map.get(&1), None);
assert_eq!(map.get(&2), Some(&20));
```
Removes the last entry.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert(1, 10);
map.insert(2, 20);
map.pop_back();
assert_eq!(map.get(&1), Some(&10));
assert_eq!(map.get(&2), None);
```
Returns a double-ended iterator visiting all key-value pairs in order of insertion.
Iterator element type is `(&'a K, &'a V)`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert("a", 10);
map.insert("c", 30);
map.insert("b", 20);
let mut iter = map.iter();
assert_eq!((&"a", &10), iter.next().unwrap());
assert_eq!((&"c", &30), iter.next().unwrap());
assert_eq!((&"b", &20), iter.next().unwrap());
assert_eq!(None, iter.next());
```
Returns a double-ended iterator visiting all key-value pairs in order of insertion.
Iterator element type is `(&'a K, &'a mut V)`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert("a", 10);
map.insert("c", 30);
map.insert("b", 20);
{
    let mut iter = map.iter_mut();
    let mut entry = iter.next().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(&"a", entry.0);
    *entry.1 = 17;
}
assert_eq!(&17, map.get(&"a").unwrap());
```
Clears the map, returning all key-value pairs as an iterator. Keeps the allocated memory for reuse.

If the returned iterator is dropped before being fully consumed, it drops the remaining key-value pairs. The returned iterator keeps a mutable borrow on the vector to optimize its implementation.

Current performance implications (why to use this over into_iter()):

- Clears the inner HashMap instead of dropping it
- Puts all drained nodes in the free-list instead of deallocating them
- Avoids deallocating the sentinel node

Returns a double-ended iterator visiting all key in order of insertion.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert('a', 10);
map.insert('c', 30);
map.insert('b', 20);
let mut keys = map.keys();
assert_eq!(&'a', keys.next().unwrap());
assert_eq!(&'c', keys.next().unwrap());
assert_eq!(&'b', keys.next().unwrap());
assert_eq!(None, keys.next());
```
Returns a double-ended iterator visiting all values in order of insertion.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
map.insert('a', 10);
map.insert('c', 30);
map.insert('b', 20);
let mut values = map.values();
assert_eq!(&10, values.next().unwrap());
assert_eq!(&30, values.next().unwrap());
assert_eq!(&20, values.next().unwrap());
assert_eq!(None, values.next());
```

# Serialize in serde_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/trait.Serialize.html

```
pub trait Serialize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[serialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize)<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), S::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where S: [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html);
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html). All of
these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

`Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
type in your program. See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the
manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the [ linked-hash-map](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map) crate provides a

[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>``Serialize` for it.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.

See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the manual for more
information about how to implement this method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
// This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
impl Serialize for Person {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
        s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
        s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
        s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
        s.end()
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Deserialize in serde_core::de - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/serde_core/1.0.228/target-redirect/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html

`pub trait Deserialize<'de>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [deserialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.deserialize)<D>(deserializer: D) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, D::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)<'de>;
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be deserialized from any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Deserialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/index.html). All of these
can be deserialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called `serde_derive` to
automatically generate `Deserialize` implementations for structs and enums
in your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html) for how to
use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Deserialize` manually for
some type in your program. See the [Implementing
 Deserialize](https://serde.rs/impl-deserialize.html) section of the manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Deserialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the `linked-hash-map` crate provides a
`LinkedHashMap<K, V>` type that is deserializable by Serde because the crate
provides an implementation of `Deserialize` for it.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
borrowed by `Self` when deserialized. See the page [Understanding
deserializer lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html) for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Deserializing a data structure containing `Rc` will not attempt to
deduplicate `Rc` references to the same data. Every deserialized `Rc`
will end up with a strong count of 1.
